narrative.h2: A tribute video that holds up to repeated watching

sections.heading: Why the memorial MV is its own format
sections.body: Funeral slideshows are usually thrown together in 48 hours under grief — they often default to chronological Facebook photos and a single piano track. A more considered MV, made days or weeks later, becomes the artifact the family actually returns to on birthdays, anniversaries, and the year-marks that follow. It's a different job from the service slideshow: less comprehensive, more curated, scored to the song the person actually loved rather than something generically somber.

sections.heading: The shots that always work
sections.body: Memorial filmmakers tend toward a small, repeatable vocabulary: the still-life of a familiar object (a coffee mug, glasses on a book, a guitar against a wall), the handwriting close-up, hands at a hobby, the laugh photo from every reunion, the chair they always sat in. The aesthetic references are quiet and specific - Bill Viola's slow-motion video installations at the Getty and Tate Modern, Sigur Ros' Hoppipolla directed by Arni & Kinski (the funeral-montage default), Lana Del Rey's Hope Is a Dangerous Thing palette, Don Hertzfeldt's It's Such a Beautiful Day for animated grief, Terrence Malick's still-photo cutaways in The Tree of Life shot by Emmanuel Lubezki. The instinct is to use every photo ever taken - resist it. Fifteen specific images, well-paced, outperform a hundred.

sections.heading: Make it the keepsake
sections.body: Memorial MVs aren't really shared — they're held. Tunee renders a high-resolution master for family archives, a vertical version for private sending to those who couldn't attend, and a 1:1 for a memorial post on what would have been the next birthday.
